# Strategy, Competition, and Industries {#strategy-competition}

Why do pharmaceutical companies and soft-drink makers earn persistently higher
returns than airlines and steel producers? Why did U.S. airlines that met each
other on many routes charge higher fares than airlines that met only
occasionally, and why did the rest of the U.S. wireless industry follow when
T-Mobile abandoned two-year service contracts in 2013? Why do some pioneers, such
as eBay in online auctions, keep their lead for decades while others, such as
Friendster and MySpace in social networking, are overtaken by later entrants? And
why do managers invest in small pilot projects that, judged one at a time, fail
the standard net-present-value test?

Each question concerns **competitive strategy**: how firms position themselves
within industries, anticipate rivals, and decide when and how much to commit.
We begin with the industrial-organization tradition, the
**[structure-conduct-performance](#structure-conduct-performance) paradigm** and the theory of **strategic
groups**. We then examine rivalry through the empirical lens of **competitive
dynamics** and the formal lens of **[game theory](#game-theory)**. Two theories address the
timing and staging of commitments: **[first-mover advantage](#first-mover-advantage)** and **[real options](#real-options-theory)
theory**. The chapter closes with two behavioural theories of the firm's
decision process, the **[behavioral theory of the firm](#behavioral-theory-of-the-firm)** and the
**[attention-based view](#attention-based-view)**. Together they span the classic tension in strategy
between models of rational rivals and models of boundedly rational
organizations (Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-glance)).

```{r tab-sc-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "Structure-conduct-performance", "Why do some industries earn higher profits than others?", "Industry", "Mason (1939), Bain (1956)",
  "Strategic groups", "Why do clusters of firms within one industry follow similar strategies and earn different returns?", "Group within industry", "Caves & Porter (1977)",
  "Competitive dynamics", "Who attacks whom, and who responds, how fast, and how strongly?", "Firm dyad", "Chen (1996)",
  "Game theory", "What should a firm do when its payoff depends on what rivals do?", "Interacting firms", "von Neumann & Morgenstern (1944), Nash (1950)",
  "First-mover advantage", "When does entering a market first pay off?", "Firm within market", "Lieberman & Montgomery (1988)",
  "Real options theory", "How should firms invest when the future is uncertain and investments are irreversible?", "Investment project, firm", "Myers (1977), Bowman & Hurry (1993)",
  "Behavioral theory of the firm", "How do performance relative to aspirations, search, and slack shape organizational decisions?", "Organization", "Cyert & March (1963)",
  "Attention-based view", "How does the allocation of managerial attention shape what firms do?", "Organization, decision maker", "Ocasio (1997)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Chapter at a glance: theories of strategy, competition, and industries.")
```

## Structure-Conduct-Performance {#structure-conduct-performance}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** The structure of an industry (concentration, barriers to entry,
product differentiation) shapes the conduct of the firms within it (pricing,
advertising, investment), and conduct determines industry performance
(profitability and efficiency). Industry is the primary unit for explaining why
profits differ.

**Origins.** Industrial organization economics. Edward Mason's Harvard program of
industry studies [@mason1939] and Joe Bain's work on concentration and entry
barriers [@bain1951; @bain1956]. Brought into strategic management by
@porter1980 and @porter1981.

**Level of analysis.** Industry (market), with firms treated as largely
similar within it.

**Key constructs.** Seller concentration, barriers to entry (economies of scale,
product differentiation, absolute cost advantages, capital requirements), the
condition of entry, conduct, industry profitability.

**Boundary conditions.** Industry boundaries must be definable. Structure must be
relatively stable and exogenous to any single firm's conduct. The theory is weakest
when firm-level efficiency differences are large or when industries are
reshaped quickly by technology.

**Related theories.** [Five forces](#five-forces) (Section \@ref(five-forces)),
[Strategic groups](#strategic-groups),
[Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Organizational ecology](#organizational-ecology) (Section \@ref(organizational-ecology)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The structure-conduct-performance (SCP) paradigm grew out of the Harvard
industrial organization program of the 1930s. @mason1939 argued that the
policies of large firms could not be understood through perfect competition
alone and called for industry-by-industry study of how market structure
conditions business behaviour. Joe Bain, trained in the same Harvard tradition,
turned the program into a testable agenda: in U.S. manufacturing of the late
1930s, profit rates were higher in the most concentrated industries
[@bain1951].

Concentration alone, however, cannot sustain high profits if outsiders can enter
freely. @bain1956 therefore introduced the concept of the **condition of entry**:
the extent to which established firms can raise prices above the competitive
level without attracting new entrants. He identified the structural sources of
**barriers to entry**, which Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-barriers) summarises
alongside later additions. The welfare logic of the paradigm was clear: high
barriers and high concentration enable collusive or tacitly coordinated conduct,
which produces high profits at the expense of consumers. SCP research therefore
became the intellectual foundation of mid-century antitrust policy.

```{r tab-sc-barriers}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Barrier, ~`Why it deters entry`, ~`Business example`,
  "Economies of scale", "An entrant must either enter at large scale (and depress prices) or accept a cost disadvantage", "Commercial aircraft manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication",
  "Product differentiation", "Buyers prefer established brands, so entrants must spend more on advertising or accept lower prices", "Carbonated soft drinks, cigarettes, breakfast cereals",
  "Absolute cost advantages", "Incumbents control superior inputs, technology, or locations at any scale", "Patented drugs, scarce airport slots, mineral deposits",
  "Capital requirements", "Large up-front investment raises financing costs and risk for entrants", "Wireless spectrum and networks, steel mills",
  "Switching costs (later addition)", "Buyers incur costs to change suppliers, locking in installed bases", "Enterprise software, banking relationships",
  "Network effects (later addition)", "The value of joining rises with the number of existing users", "Payment networks, marketplaces, social platforms"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Barriers to entry in the SCP tradition. The first four follow Bain (1956). The last two are later additions emphasised in strategy and platform research.")
```

### Core logic and propositions

The paradigm runs from structure to conduct to performance, with basic
conditions of supply and demand (technology, demand elasticity, growth) at the
start of the chain. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-scp) shows the logic, including the
feedback loops that later critics emphasised.

```{r fig-sc-scp, fig.cap = "The structure-conduct-performance paradigm. Basic conditions shape market structure, which shapes firm conduct and, in turn, industry performance. Dashed arrows show the feedback effects (conduct reshaping structure, and performance attracting entry) stressed by later work."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  B [label = "Basic conditions\\n(technology, demand,\\ngrowth, elasticity)", %s]
  S [label = "Market structure\\n(concentration, entry\\nbarriers, differentiation)", %s]
  C [label = "Conduct\\n(pricing, advertising,\\ncapacity, R&D)", %s]
  P [label = "Performance\\n(profitability,\\nefficiency)", %s]
  G [label = "Public policy\\n(antitrust, regulation)", %s]
  B -> S -> C -> P
  C -> S [style = dashed, label = " entry deterrence,\\n mergers", constraint = false]
  P -> S [style = dashed, label = " profits attract\\n entry", constraint = false]
  G -> S [style = dotted]
  G -> C [style = dotted]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

The paradigm can be stated as four propositions:

- **P1 (Concentration).** Industries with higher seller concentration earn higher
  average profits, because fewer sellers find it easier to coordinate, tacitly or
  explicitly [@bain1951].
- **P2 (Entry barriers).** High concentration translates into persistent profits
  only when barriers to entry are high [@bain1956].
- **P3 (Industry primacy).** Because structure constrains conduct, industry
  membership explains a substantial share of the variance in firm profitability.
- **P4 (Strategic inversion).** For a firm, the attractive course is to enter
  industries with favourable structure or to reshape structure in its favour,
  the inversion of the paradigm's welfare logic that @porter1981 made the basis
  of competitive strategy.

That inversion is the paradigm's most consequential legacy for business. Where
the antitrust economist saw high barriers as a social cost, @porter1980 saw them
as a source of protected returns, and organized industry analysis into the
[five forces](#five-forces) (Section \@ref(five-forces)) framework: rivalry, threat of entry, threat of
substitutes, and the bargaining power of buyers and suppliers [@porter1979].

### Evidence and extensions

The SCP paradigm met two major challenges. The first came from the Chicago
school. @demsetz1973 argued that the correlation between concentration and
profits might reflect efficiency rather than collusion: if a few firms are
genuinely better, they will grow large, the industry will become concentrated,
and their superior profits will raise the industry average. Market power predicts
that *all* firms in a concentrated industry gain. Efficiency predicts that mainly
the large, efficient firms do. Demsetz reported evidence more consistent with the
second view, opening a debate about whether profits reflect market power or
superior capability that continues in [resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)).

The second challenge came from variance decomposition. If structure drives
profitability, industry membership should explain much of the variation in
business-unit returns. @schmalensee1985, using a single year of U.S. Federal
Trade Commission line-of-business data, found that industry effects accounted
for about a fifth of that variance, whereas corporate and market share effects
were negligible or small. @rumelt1991 used several years of the same data,
which allowed him to separate stable business-unit effects from industry
effects. Business-unit effects were several times larger than stable industry
effects, a result widely read as evidence that firm-specific resources and
strategies matter more than industry. @mcgahan1997 and @hawawini2003 qualified
the conclusion, as Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-variance) summarises, and Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-sc-variance) stylises the contrast between the two research
designs.

```{r fig-sc-variance, fig.cap = "Stylised variance decomposition of business-unit profitability. A single-year design cannot separate business-unit effects from noise, so industry appears to be the main systematic source of profit differences. A multi-year design isolates stable business-unit effects, which then dominate. Shares are illustrative and are not the published estimates of any one study.", fig.height = 4.2}
decomp <- tibble::tribble(
  ~design, ~component, ~share,
  "Single-year design\n(Schmalensee-type)", "Industry", 20,
  "Single-year design\n(Schmalensee-type)", "Corporate parent", 1,
  "Single-year design\n(Schmalensee-type)", "Business unit", 0,
  "Single-year design\n(Schmalensee-type)", "Unexplained", 79,
  "Multi-year design\n(Rumelt-type)", "Industry", 9,
  "Multi-year design\n(Rumelt-type)", "Corporate parent", 2,
  "Multi-year design\n(Rumelt-type)", "Business unit", 45,
  "Multi-year design\n(Rumelt-type)", "Unexplained", 44
) |>
  mutate(component = factor(component, levels = c("Unexplained", "Business unit", "Corporate parent", "Industry")),
         design = factor(design, levels = rev(unique(design))))
ggplot(decomp, aes(share, design, fill = component)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_text(data = filter(decomp, share >= 5), aes(label = paste0(share, "%")),
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3.4, colour = "white", fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Industry" = pal[["blue"]], "Corporate parent" = pal[["orange"]],
                               "Business unit" = pal[["aqua"]], "Unexplained" = "#c9c8c3"),
                    breaks = c("Industry", "Corporate parent", "Business unit", "Unexplained")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) paste0(x, "%"), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Share of variance in business-unit profitability", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "How much does industry matter?",
       subtitle = "The answer depends on whether the design can isolate stable business-unit effects",
       caption = "Stylised shares, broadly in the spirit of Schmalensee (1985) and Rumelt (1991). Not empirical estimates.")
```

```{r tab-sc-variance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Study, ~Data, ~`Headline finding`, ~`Interpretation`,
  "Schmalensee (1985)", "FTC line-of-business data, single year", "Industry effects explain about a fifth of the variance, corporate effects negligible", "Supports the industry focus of SCP",
  "Rumelt (1991)", "FTC line-of-business data, several years", "Stable business-unit effects are far larger than stable industry effects", "Firm-specific strategy and resources matter most",
  "McGahan & Porter (1997)", "Compustat business segments, 1981-1994", "Industry about 19 percent, business-specific about 32 percent, corporate about 4 percent", "Industry still matters, and its importance varies by sector",
  "Hawawini, Subramanian & Verdin (2003)", "Value-based performance measures such as economic profit", "Firm effects dominate for leaders and laggards, industry effects matter more for average firms", "The answer depends on where a firm sits in its industry"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Key variance-decomposition studies of firm profitability.")
```

::: {.debate}
**Market power or efficiency?** The SCP paradigm treats structure as exogenous,
but efficient firms grow and make industries concentrated [@demsetz1973].
Variance-decomposition results depend on the sample, the performance measure,
and whether stable and transient effects are separated
[@rumelt1991; @mcgahan1997; @hawawini2003]. Moreover, decomposing variance says
nothing about *causal mechanisms*: a large business-unit effect is a residual
that could reflect resources, skill, luck, or a favourable niche. Most scholars
now treat industry and firm effects as complementary explanations.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Why airlines struggle and soft drinks thrive.** The U.S. airline industry is a
classic case of unfavourable structure. Aircraft and airport access can be leased,
so capital barriers are lower than they appear, fixed costs are high and marginal
costs per seat are low, products are hard to differentiate, and buyers compare
fares instantly. The industry's long history of bankruptcies and consolidation is
what SCP would predict. Carbonated soft drinks show the opposite configuration:
strong brands built over a century, bottler networks, and shelf and fountain
contracts create formidable barriers, and the industry is dominated by two firms.
The same paradigm explains why airlines have pursued consolidation, loyalty
programmes, and control of hub airports: each is an attempt to change structure
rather than merely to compete within it.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Industry concentration will be positively associated with price-cost
  margins, and the association will be stronger when entry barriers (measured by
  minimum efficient scale relative to market size) are high.
- *H2.* The share of variance in business-unit returns explained by industry
  effects will be larger in regulated and capital-intensive industries than in
  fragmented service industries.

**Measures.** Concentration ratios (CR4, CR8) and the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index,
minimum efficient scale, advertising and R&D intensity, price-cost margins,
return on assets, Tobin's q.

**Designs.** Variance decomposition with random-effects or multilevel models
(Compustat segments, census concentration data), and within-industry natural
experiments such as deregulation, patent expiries, and entry shocks.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating industry definitions as given.** Industry codes are administrative
categories, not markets. A four-digit code may lump together firms that do not
compete (luxury and economy hotels) and separate firms that do (streaming
services and cable television). Concentration measured at the wrong boundary is
meaningless. Define the relevant market by substitution patterns before
computing structure, and test the sensitivity of results to alternative
definitions.
:::

## Strategic Groups {#strategic-groups}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Within an industry, firms cluster into **strategic groups** that
follow similar strategies along key dimensions. Groups are protected from one
another by **mobility barriers**, which can sustain profit differences between
groups within the same industry.

**Origins.** Industrial organization and strategic management. The term
originated in doctoral research on the U.S. home-appliance industry in the early
1970s. The theory of mobility barriers was developed by @caves1977 and
@porter1980. Empirical and cognitive extensions by @cool1987, @porac1989, and
@reger1993.

**Level of analysis.** Groups of firms within an industry.

**Key constructs.** Strategic dimensions (scope, resource commitments), strategic
group, mobility barriers, within-group rivalry, between-group rivalry,
cognitive groups.

**Boundary conditions.** Firms must differ systematically along a small number of
costly-to-change strategic dimensions. If strategies are easy to imitate,
groups dissolve and mobility barriers vanish.

**Related theories.** [Structure-conduct-performance](#structure-conduct-performance),
[Competitive dynamics](#competitive-dynamics),
[Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Institutional theory](#institutional-theory) (Section \@ref(institutional-theory)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

The SCP paradigm treated firms in an industry as similar, but in home appliances
full-line national brands, private-label suppliers, and narrow specialists faced
the same structure yet behaved and performed differently. @caves1977 generalised
Bain's entry barriers into **mobility barriers**, which deter firms from moving
between strategic groups as well as from entering the industry. A national
brand, a dealer network, or a patent portfolio protects its owners from both
outsiders and insiders in other groups. Because firms invest deliberately in
such barriers, they are partly a product of strategy rather than a fixed
feature of structure.

The theory yields four propositions:

- **P1 (Clustering).** Firms cluster along a few strategic dimensions, such as
  product scope, vertical integration, brand investment, and geographic reach.
- **P2 (Mobility barriers).** Moving between groups requires costly, slow, or
  uncertain investments, so membership persists [@caves1977].
- **P3 (Performance differences).** Groups protected by higher mobility barriers
  earn higher returns.
- **P4 (Rivalry structure).** Rivalry is usually most intense within groups,
  and rivalry between groups depends on how much their markets overlap.

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-groups) shows an illustrative strategic group map for
a stylised airline industry.

```{r fig-sc-groups, fig.cap = "Illustrative strategic group map of a stylised airline industry. Firms cluster on network breadth and service bundle. Mobility barriers, such as hub slots and long-haul fleets, separate full-service network carriers from low-cost and ultra-low-cost carriers. Simulated data.", fig.height = 4.4}
set.seed(1977)
groups <- tibble::tibble(
  group = rep(c("Full-service network carriers", "Low-cost carriers", "Ultra-low-cost carriers"), times = c(6, 8, 7)),
  cx = rep(c(80, 45, 25), times = c(6, 8, 7)),
  cy = rep(c(78, 45, 18), times = c(6, 8, 7))
) |>
  mutate(breadth = cx + rnorm(n(), 0, 6), service = cy + rnorm(n(), 0, 6),
         size = runif(n(), 1, 6))
ggplot(groups, aes(breadth, service, colour = group)) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(fill = group), geom = "polygon", alpha = 0.08, level = 0.95, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(size = size), alpha = 0.85) +
  annotate("text", x = 84, y = 33, label ="Mobility barrier:\nhub slots, long-haul fleet,\nglobal alliance", size = 3,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = 0.5) +
  annotate("text", x = 16, y = 58, label ="Mobility barrier:\ncost structure,\nlabour contracts", size = 3,
           colour = ink[["secondary"]], hjust = 0.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]])) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]]), guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 5), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(x = "Network breadth (index)", y = "Service bundle and amenities (index)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Strategic groups in a stylised airline industry",
       caption = "Illustrative simulated data. Point size indicates relative market share.") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 1, override.aes = list(size = 3)))
```

### Evidence and extensions

Strategic groups are easy to *find* with cluster analysis but harder to
*validate*. @cool1987 studied the U.S. pharmaceutical industry from 1963 to 1982,
defining groups by scope and resource commitments and identifying periods of
stable group structure. Their results, like much subsequent work, suggested that
performance differences between groups were less systematic than the
mobility-barrier argument implied, and they later examined performance
differences *within* groups [@cool1988]. @barney1990 argued that the literature
rested on two untested assertions: that groups exist as more than statistical
artefacts, and that performance depends on group membership.

A productive response came from the cognitive tradition. @porac1989 showed that
Scottish knitwear manufacturers defined their rivals narrowly, as other
high-end classic knitwear producers in their region, and largely ignored the
mass-market producers who dominated global volume. @reger1993 found that bank
executives perceived consistent cognitive groupings of their rivals. Cognitive
groups explain why firms watch some rivals closely and ignore others, linking the
theory to the [attention-based view](#attention-based-view).

::: {.debate}
**Real structures or analyst constructs?** Cluster algorithms will always
produce clusters, so the existence of groups cannot be inferred from clustering
alone [@barney1990]. Critics also note that groups are defined on strategic
choices and then used to explain performance, which invites circularity when the
choices themselves respond to performance. Defenders reply that groups are
useful when they are defined *ex ante* on theoretically motivated dimensions,
validated against managers' own perceptions [@reger1993], and used to predict
behaviour such as rivalry and response patterns rather than only profits.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Airline strategic groups.** U.S. aviation offers a well-documented example of
strategic groups. Legacy network carriers operate hub-and-spoke systems, long-haul
international fleets, global alliances, and multi-class cabins. Low-cost carriers
historically offered point-to-point service, a single aircraft type, and a
simpler product, while ultra-low-cost carriers unbundle almost everything beyond
the seat. Mobility barriers run in both directions: low-cost carriers cannot
easily acquire congested hub slots or long-haul networks, and network carriers
cannot easily replicate low-cost labour contracts and simplified operations. The
network carriers' introduction of "basic economy" fares in the 2010s can be read as
an attempt to compete with the lower groups without crossing the mobility
barrier.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Firms will respond more quickly to competitive moves by members of their
  own strategic group than to moves by firms in other groups.
- *H2.* The performance gap between strategic groups will be larger in
  industries where the investments that define groups are less reversible.
- *H3.* Managers' cognitive groupings of rivals will predict competitive
  responses better than groupings derived from cluster analysis of financial
  data.

**Measures.** Strategic dimensions (product scope, advertising intensity, R&D
intensity, vertical integration, geographic scope), mobility barrier proxies (sunk
investments, regulatory licences), cognitive maps elicited from managers through
repertory grids or rival-naming tasks.

**Designs.** Cluster analysis with *ex ante* dimensions and stability tests,
multilevel models of performance (firm within group within industry), event
studies of group entry and exit, and text analysis of annual reports to recover
self-defined competitor sets.
:::

## Competitive Dynamics {#competitive-dynamics}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Competition is a sequence of actions and responses between
specific rivals. Whether a firm attacks a rival, and whether and how a rival
responds, depends on the pair's **market commonality** and **resource
similarity**, which shape each firm's **awareness**, **motivation**, and
**capability** to act. Firms that meet in many markets often compete less
aggressively because of **mutual forbearance**.

**Origins.** Strategic management, building on Austrian economics and
industrial organization. @chen1992, @chen1996, and the review by @chen2012.
Multimarket contact and mutual forbearance: @karnani1985, @bernheim1990,
@gimeno1996.

**Level of analysis.** The competitive dyad (a pair of rivals), and the actions
and responses between them.

**Key constructs.** Competitive action and response, market commonality,
resource similarity, competitor asymmetry, awareness, motivation, capability
(AMC), multimarket contact, mutual forbearance, spheres of influence.

**Boundary conditions.** Rivals must be able to observe each other's actions and
to respond. The theory is most informative in industries with frequent,
identifiable moves (price changes, product launches, route entries).

**Related theories.** [Game theory](#game-theory),
[Strategic groups](#strategic-groups),
[Attention-based view](#attention-based-view),
[Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Classic industry analysis treats competition as a property of markets.
Competitive dynamics research, which emerged in the late 1980s, treats it as a
series of concrete moves (a price cut, a new route, a product launch) and the
replies they provoke, often coded from trade publications on U.S. airlines.
@chen1992 found that actions affecting many competitors drew more responses,
whereas **strategic actions** (large, hard-to-reverse commitments) drew fewer
and slower responses than **tactical actions** such as price changes.
@miller1994 linked past success to **competitive inertia**, a narrower and less
changeable competitive repertoire.

### Core logic and propositions

@chen1996 integrated this work into a theory of **competitor analysis** built on
two dyad-level constructs. **Market commonality** is the degree to which a
competitor is present in the markets that matter to the focal firm. **Resource
similarity** is the extent to which a competitor's strategic endowments resemble
the focal firm's in type and amount. Because each firm's market portfolio differs,
the two constructs are **asymmetric**: Firm A may be Firm B's main rival while B
is a minor concern for A. These constructs operate through three behavioural
drivers, known as the **awareness-motivation-capability** (AMC) perspective
[@chen1996; @chen2012]. A firm attacks or responds only if it is *aware* of the
rival or the move, *motivated* to act (because the stakes are high), and *capable*
of acting (because it has the resources).

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-amc) summarises the mechanism.

```{r fig-sc-amc, fig.cap = "Competitive dynamics mechanism. Market commonality and resource similarity shape a firm's awareness of, motivation toward, and capability against a rival. These drivers determine the likelihood of attack and the likelihood, speed, and strength of response. Multimarket contact can temper rivalry through mutual forbearance."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  MC [label = "Market\\ncommonality", %s]
  RS [label = "Resource\\nsimilarity", %s]
  A  [label = "Awareness", %s]
  M  [label = "Motivation", %s]
  C  [label = "Capability", %s]
  AT [label = "Likelihood\\nof attack", %s]
  RE [label = "Likelihood, speed,\\nand strength of response", %s]
  MF [label = "Multimarket contact\\n(mutual forbearance)", %s]
  MC -> A
  MC -> M
  RS -> A
  RS -> C
  A -> AT
  M -> AT
  C -> AT
  A -> RE
  M -> RE
  C -> RE
  MF -> AT [style = dashed, label = " tempers"]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

The central propositions are:

- **P1 (Attack deterrence).** A firm is less likely to attack a rival with high
  market commonality, because the rival is highly motivated to retaliate across
  the many markets they share [@chen1996].
- **P2 (Response likelihood).** A firm is more likely to respond to an attack by a
  rival with high market commonality, because the attack threatens markets that
  matter to it.
- **P3 (Capability).** Resource similarity raises the rival's capability to
  respond in kind, which makes attack less attractive and response more feasible.
- **P4 (Action characteristics).** Responses are more likely and faster for
  visible, easily reversed, tactical actions than for complex, irreversible,
  strategic actions [@chen1992].
- **P5 (Mutual forbearance).** Firms that meet in many markets compete less
  aggressively in each, because aggression in one market invites retaliation in
  others [@karnani1985; @bernheim1990].

Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-amc) translates the constructs into measures.

```{r tab-sc-amc}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Construct, ~Definition, ~`Typical measure`,
  "Market commonality", "Overlap of a rival in markets that matter to the focal firm, weighted by importance", "Share of focal firm's revenue earned in markets where the rival is present",
  "Resource similarity", "Comparability of strategic endowments in type and amount", "Distance in resource profiles (fleet, assets, capabilities)",
  "Awareness", "Degree to which a firm notices a rival or its move", "Visibility of the action, analyst or media coverage, managerial mentions",
  "Motivation", "Perceived stakes of acting or responding", "Revenue at risk in the attacked market",
  "Capability", "Resources available to act or respond", "Slack, scale, product breadth",
  "Multimarket contact", "Number of markets in which two firms meet", "Count or share of overlapping routes, regions, or product markets",
  "Response", "A counter-move aimed at the attacker", "Coded from trade press, response lag in days, number of responders"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Key constructs in competitive dynamics research and typical operationalizations.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The theory has strong empirical support in industries where moves can be
observed. In airlines, @evans1994 found that fares were higher on routes served
by carriers that met each other in many other markets, consistent with mutual
forbearance. @gimeno1999 showed that airlines with dominant positions in each
other's hubs tended to respect one another's **spheres of influence**, and
@gimeno1996 found that multimarket contact de-escalated rivalry, whereas
strategic similarity intensified it. @baum1996 showed that market domain overlap
and multimarket contact jointly shaped entry and exit among California commuter
airlines. The formal foundation came from @bernheim1990, who showed that
multimarket contact helps sustain collusion by pooling incentive constraints
across markets: when markets or firms differ, slack in one market's incentive to
cooperate can be transferred to another. When all markets and firms are
identical, multimarket contact adds nothing. That result is an important
boundary condition.

::: {.debate}
**Forbearance or collusion?** Mutual forbearance raises a normative question
that matters for merger review: is it efficient coexistence or tacit collusion
that harms customers? Measurement is also contested, because actions coded from
trade publications over-represent visible, newsworthy moves. Finally, the dyadic
focus can neglect the wider network of rivals, who also observe every response
[@chen2012].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Fare wars and spheres of influence in airlines.** Airline competition offers a
textbook record of action and response. In the spring of 1992, American
Airlines introduced a simplified "Value Pricing" fare structure. Rivals answered
with promotions of their own, and by the summer the industry was locked in a broad
fare war that deepened losses across the sector. The episode illustrates P2 and
P4: fare changes are visible, easy to reverse, and threaten rivals in many shared
markets, so responses come quickly. By contrast, carriers have generally avoided
head-on attacks on each other's fortress hubs, consistent with the spheres of
influence documented by @gimeno1999.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**The Un-carrier and wireless rivalry.** In 2013, T-Mobile US, then the
fourth-largest U.S. wireless carrier, launched its "Un-carrier" strategy, beginning
with the elimination of two-year service contracts and continuing with a sequence
of publicly announced moves on pricing and plan features. The AMC perspective
explains both the attack and the responses. As the smallest national carrier,
T-Mobile had little to lose from disrupting industry pricing norms. Its moves
were highly visible and threatened larger rivals' core subscriber bases, and
those rivals also moved away from traditional contracts over the following
years. Verizon reintroduced an unlimited data plan in early 2017.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The likelihood that a firm responds to a rival's price cut will increase
  with the rival's market commonality with the focal firm.
- *H2.* Multimarket contact between two firms will be negatively associated with
  the frequency of price cuts in their shared markets, and the association will
  be stronger when the firms differ in market positions (asymmetric spheres of
  influence).

**Measures.** Structured content analysis of trade press for actions and
responses, response lag, number of responders, market commonality and resource
similarity indices, multimarket contact counts at the dyad level.

**Designs.** Dyad-level panel models, hazard models of response timing, and
natural experiments from mergers that change multimarket overlap, using sources
such as airline route and fare data, wireless plan histories, and retail price
scrapes.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Ignoring asymmetry.** A frequent error is to treat rivalry as symmetric, for
example by computing a single overlap measure for a pair of firms. Market
commonality and resource similarity are directional: what matters for the focal
firm's behaviour is how much of *its* business the rival touches, not the
reverse. Use directed dyads and test whether predictions hold separately for
each direction.
:::

## Game Theory {#game-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** When the payoff of each actor depends on the choices of others,
rational strategy requires anticipating rivals' responses. Outcomes can be
predicted as **equilibria**, combinations of strategies from which no player
gains by deviating unilaterally.

**Origins.** Mathematics and economics. @vonneumann1944 founded the field. @nash1950
and @nash1951 defined the equilibrium concept that bears his name. Applications
to business strategy include @schelling1960 on commitment, @dixit1980 on entry
deterrence, @tirole1988 on industrial organization, and @brandenburger1996 on
co-opetition.

**Level of analysis.** Interacting decision makers: firms in an oligopoly,
negotiating parties, platform and complementors.

**Key constructs.** Players, strategies, payoffs, information, Nash equilibrium,
dominant strategy, prisoner's dilemma, Cournot and Bertrand competition,
sequential moves, commitment, credibility, repeated games, reputation, added
value.

**Boundary conditions.** The number of relevant players is small enough that
interdependence is recognised. Players are assumed to understand the game and to
reason strategically. Predictions are sensitive to the timing of moves, the
information structure, and the equilibrium concept chosen.

**Related theories.** [Competitive dynamics](#competitive-dynamics),
[Collective action](#collective-action) (Section \@ref(collective-action)),
[Auction theory](#auction-theory) (Section \@ref(auction-theory)),
[Two-sided markets](#two-sided-markets) (Section \@ref(two-sided-markets)),
[Signaling theory](#signaling-theory) (Section \@ref(signaling-theory)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@vonneumann1944 established game theory as a formal discipline, solving
two-person zero-sum games. Most business situations, however, are not zero-sum:
firms can both gain from restraint or both lose from a price war. @nash1950
proved that every finite game has at least one equilibrium (possibly in mixed
strategies) in which each player's strategy is a best response to the others',
opening the analysis of non-cooperative games [@nash1951]. Older oligopoly
models, Cournot's (1838) firms choosing quantities and Bertrand's (1883) firms
undercutting each other's prices down to marginal cost, were recast as Nash
equilibria and extended to sequential moves, incomplete information, and
repeated interaction [@tirole1988; @shapiro1989theory].

### Core logic: the prisoner's dilemma

The **prisoner's dilemma** is the canonical structure behind many competitive
traps. Each firm has a dominant strategy to defect (cut price, increase
advertising), yet both would be better off if both cooperated. Table
\@ref(tab:tab-sc-pd) presents an illustrative pricing game between two
soft-drink rivals.

```{r tab-sc-pd}
tibble::tribble(
  ~` `, ~`Pepsi holds price`, ~`Pepsi discounts`,
  "Coca-Cola holds price", "10, 10 (joint best)", "2, 14",
  "Coca-Cola discounts", "14, 2", "5, 5 (Nash equilibrium)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Illustrative scenario: a pricing prisoner's dilemma between two cola rivals. Cells show (Coca-Cola payoff, Pepsi payoff) in stylised profit units. Discounting is each firm's dominant strategy, so the one-shot equilibrium is mutual discounting even though mutual restraint pays both more.", align = "lcc")
```

Whatever Pepsi does, Coca-Cola earns more by discounting (14 > 10 and 5 > 2), and
the same holds for Pepsi. The unique Nash equilibrium is mutual discounting, with
payoffs of 5 each, although both would earn 10 under mutual restraint. The game
explains why industries with few rivals do not automatically enjoy monopoly
profits and why price wars, advertising escalation, and capacity races can
persist even when every participant regrets them.

### Core logic: from one-shot to repeated games

Real rivals meet repeatedly. In a repeated game, cooperation can be sustained if
each firm credibly threatens to punish defection and if the future matters enough.
With a "grim trigger" strategy (cooperate until the rival defects, then defect
forever), cooperation is an equilibrium when the discount factor $\delta$ satisfies
$\delta \geq (T - R)/(T - P)$, where $T$ is the temptation payoff, $R$ the reward for
mutual cooperation, and $P$ the punishment payoff. With the payoffs in Table
\@ref(tab:tab-sc-pd), this threshold is $(14 - 10)/(14 - 5) \approx 0.44$. This
logic underlies the **folk theorems** of repeated games and the forbearance
results of the previous section.

@axelrod1984 ran computer tournaments in which strategies submitted by
researchers played a repeated prisoner's dilemma. The simplest entry, **tit for
tat** (cooperate first, then copy the rival's last move), won. It was nice (never
defected first), retaliatory, forgiving, and clear. In noisy environments, where
moves are sometimes misread or mistakes occur, strict retaliation can trigger
long echoes of punishment. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-repeated) simulates this
problem.

```{r fig-sc-repeated, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of a repeated pricing game with noise. Each period, each firm's intended move is reversed with probability 0.05 (a mistake or a misread price). Grim trigger collapses into permanent price war after the first error. Tit for tat sustains less cooperation than it does without noise because errors echo back and forth. Generous tit for tat, which forgives a defection one-third of the time, recovers cooperation quickly.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1984)
sim_game <- function(rule, n_sims = 2000, rounds = 60, noise = 0.05, generosity = 1/3) {
  a_prev <- rep(1, n_sims); b_prev <- rep(1, n_sims)        # 1 = cooperate (hold price)
  triggered <- rep(FALSE, n_sims)
  out <- numeric(rounds)
  for (t in seq_len(rounds)) {
    if (rule == "Grim trigger") {
      a_int <- ifelse(triggered, 0, 1); b_int <- a_int
    } else if (rule == "Tit for tat") {
      a_int <- b_prev; b_int <- a_prev
    } else {
      a_int <- ifelse(b_prev == 1, 1, rbinom(n_sims, 1, generosity))
      b_int <- ifelse(a_prev == 1, 1, rbinom(n_sims, 1, generosity))
    }
    a_err <- rbinom(n_sims, 1, noise) == 1
    b_err <- rbinom(n_sims, 1, noise) == 1
    a_act <- ifelse(a_err, 1 - a_int, a_int)
    b_act <- ifelse(b_err, 1 - b_int, b_int)
    triggered <- triggered | a_act == 0 | b_act == 0
    out[t] <- mean(a_act == 1 & b_act == 1)
    a_prev <- a_act; b_prev <- b_act
  }
  tibble::tibble(rule = rule, round = seq_len(rounds), coop = out)
}
rep_game <- bind_rows(lapply(c("Grim trigger", "Tit for tat", "Generous tit for tat"), sim_game)) |>
  mutate(rule = factor(rule, levels = c("Generous tit for tat", "Tit for tat", "Grim trigger")))
ggplot(rep_game, aes(round, coop, colour = rule)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Generous tit for tat" = pal[["aqua"]], "Tit for tat" = pal[["blue"]],
                                 "Grim trigger" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Period of repeated interaction", y = "Share of rival pairs both holding price", colour = NULL,
       title = "Forgiveness sustains cooperation when moves are noisy",
       caption = "Illustrative simulation: 2,000 rival pairs per rule, 60 periods, 5% chance of a mistaken move per firm per period.")
```

### Core logic: commitment and the timing of moves

When moves are sequential, the first mover can shape the rival's choices by
**commitment**: an irreversible action that changes its own future incentives.
@schelling1960 showed that limiting one's own options can pay if it makes
threats credible. In @dixit1980, an incumbent that invests in capacity before
entry lowers its marginal cost of expanding output, which makes aggressive
post-entry pricing credible and can deter entry. @ghemawat1991 argued that
strategy turns on a small number of such **sticky, lumpy, irreversible**
commitments. **Reputation** works similarly: even a small probability that an
incumbent is a "tough" type can make it rational to fight early entrants and so
deter later ones [@kreps1982; @milgrom1982b].

Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-games) maps the main models to business situations.

```{r tab-sc-games}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Model, ~`Strategic variable`, ~`Key prediction`, ~`Business situation`,
  "Prisoner's dilemma", "Cooperate or defect", "Mutual defection in one-shot play", "Price wars, advertising escalation, promotions",
  "Cournot oligopoly", "Quantities or capacity", "Prices above cost, falling as rivals increase", "Commodity chemicals, memory chips, oil output",
  "Bertrand competition", "Prices for similar products", "Prices driven toward marginal cost", "Online retail of identical goods, generic drugs",
  "Stackelberg leadership", "Sequential quantity choice", "The leader commits to large output and gains", "Capacity pre-emption by incumbents",
  "Entry deterrence", "Capacity, pricing, reputation", "Credible commitments deter entrants", "Incumbent investment ahead of demand",
  "Repeated games", "Strategies over time", "Cooperation if the future matters enough", "Tacit price coordination, mutual forbearance",
  "Co-opetition (value net)", "Players, added values, rules, tactics, scope", "Change the game rather than play it better", "Complementors in platforms, joint standards"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Game-theoretic models and the business situations they illuminate.")
```

### Co-opetition and changing the game

@brandenburger1996 translated game theory for managers through two ideas. The
**value net** maps a firm's customers, suppliers, competitors, and
**complementors** (players whose products make the firm's products more
valuable), and the same firm can be both competitor and complementor. **Added
value** is the amount by which total value would fall if a player left the game,
and no player can capture more than its added value. The lesson is that firms
often gain more by *changing the game* (its players, added values, rules,
tactics, and scope) than by playing it more cleverly.

::: {.debate}
**Is game theory useful for strategy?** @saloner1991 defended formal models as
disciplined thought experiments even when they yield no precise prescription.
@camerer1991 noted that predictions hinge on assumptions about rationality and
common knowledge that experiments often contradict. A further criticism is that
almost any outcome can be rationalised by some game, so the game must be
specified before the data are examined. Defenders reply that the theory's value
lies in diagnosing the *structure* of a situation, which then guides action.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**The cola wars as a repeated game.** Coca-Cola and PepsiCo have competed in
carbonated soft drinks for more than a century, a textbook repeated game between
two dominant players. Their rivalry has been conducted mostly through
advertising, brand campaigns, and contracts with restaurant chains and bottlers
rather than through sustained list-price wars. Pepsi's blind-taste "Pepsi
Challenge," launched in the 1970s, was a highly visible attack. Coca-Cola's
decision in April 1985 to replace its flagship formula with "New Coke," widely
interpreted as a reaction to Pepsi's gains in taste tests, provoked a consumer
backlash, and within about three months the original formula
returned as "Coca-Cola Classic." In game-theoretic terms, heavy advertising has
some prisoner's-dilemma features (each firm advertises partly to neutralise the
other), while restraint in price competition is consistent with the repeated-game
logic of Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-repeated).
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: credible capacity commitment.** A regional cement
producer learns that a rival plans to build a plant in its market. If the
incumbent announces a price war, the threat is not credible: once the entrant
has sunk its investment, fighting would hurt the incumbent too. If the incumbent
instead completes a capacity expansion *before* the entrant decides, the
calculation changes. With low marginal cost on its new capacity, the incumbent
will rationally price aggressively after entry, and the entrant, anticipating
this, may stay out [@dixit1980]. The commitment works only because it is
irreversible and observable.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Price cooperation among rivals will be greater in markets where firms
  expect to interact for longer (for example, lower probability of exit).
- *H2.* Incumbents will invest more in capacity ahead of demand in markets where
  the threat of entry is high and capacity is irreversible.
- *H3.* In laboratory pricing games, the introduction of noise in observed rival
  prices will reduce cooperation more under strict tit for tat than under
  forgiving strategies.

**Designs.** Formal modelling to derive predictions, structural estimation of
oligopoly conduct, laboratory and online experiments with repeated games, and
quasi-experiments from changes in information (price transparency regulation,
public price comparison sites).

**Measures.** Price-cost margins, price dispersion, frequency and depth of price
cuts, capacity announcements, entry and exit, and experimentally elicited
cooperation rates.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Reasoning from the wrong game.** The most common misuse is to apply a
familiar game (usually the prisoner's dilemma) without checking that its
assumptions hold. Are moves simultaneous or sequential? Is the interaction
one-shot or repeated? Are payoffs known? Can commitments be observed? A
Bertrand model predicts cut-throat pricing, a Cournot model moderate margins,
and a repeated game possible cooperation, all for the same industry. Specify the
game from institutional facts before deriving a prediction.
:::

## First-Mover Advantage {#first-mover-advantage}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Pioneering firms can earn positive economic profits because early
entry allows them to gain technological leadership, pre-empt scarce assets, and
create buyer switching costs. Early entry also carries disadvantages, so the net
advantage depends on the firm's resources and on how fast technology and markets
evolve.

**Origins.** Strategic management and marketing. @lieberman1988 and
@lieberman1998. Marketing evidence from @robinson1985, @carpenter1989, and the
critique by @golder1993. [Contingency theory](#contingency-theory) (Section \@ref(contingency-theory)) of entry timing by @suarez2007.

**Level of analysis.** Firm within a new product market.

**Key constructs.** Order of entry, pioneer, early follower, technological
leadership, pre-emption of assets, switching costs, free-rider effects,
resolution of uncertainty, incumbent inertia, pace of technological and market
evolution.

**Boundary conditions.** Advantages require mechanisms that let the pioneer
appropriate value (learning that stays proprietary, scarce assets, switching
costs, [network effects](#network-effects) (Section \@ref(network-effects))). They weaken when technology or customer needs shift
quickly or when imitation is cheap.

**Related theories.** [Resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)),
[Network effects](#network-effects) (Section \@ref(network-effects)),
[Dominant design](#dominant-design) (Section \@ref(dominant-design)),
[Diffusion of innovations](#diffusion-of-innovations) (Section \@ref(diffusion-of-innovations)),
[Liability of newness](#liability-of-newness) (Section \@ref(liability-of-newness)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

The idea that being first pays is intuitive and was popular with managers long
before it was a theory. @lieberman1988 gave it theoretical structure by asking
*how* a pioneer could earn positive economic profits and why the advantage would
not be competed away. They identified three families of mechanisms and four
countervailing disadvantages. Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-fma) presents the
mechanism, and Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-fma) gives examples.

```{r fig-sc-fma, fig.cap = "Mechanisms of first-mover advantage and disadvantage. Early entry can generate advantages through technological leadership, pre-emption of scarce assets, and buyer switching costs, but also exposes the pioneer to free riding, unresolved uncertainty, shifts in technology or needs, and its own inertia. The pace of technological and market evolution moderates the balance."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  E  [label = "Early entry\\n(order of entry)", %s]
  T  [label = "Technological leadership\\n(learning curve, patents)", %s]
  P  [label = "Pre-emption of scarce assets\\n(inputs, locations, capacity)", %s]
  S  [label = "Buyer switching costs\\nand network effects", %s]
  F  [label = "Free-rider effects", %s]
  U  [label = "Unresolved technological\\nand market uncertainty", %s]
  I  [label = "Shifts in technology\\nor needs, incumbent inertia", %s]
  N  [label = "Net first-mover\\nadvantage (share, profit)", %s]
  D  [label = "Pace of technological\\nand market evolution", %s]
  E -> T
  E -> P
  E -> S
  E -> F
  E -> U
  E -> I
  T -> N
  P -> N
  S -> N
  F -> N [style = dashed, label = " erodes"]
  U -> N [style = dashed]
  I -> N [style = dashed]
  D -> N [style = dotted]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_moderator, node_moderator,
   node_moderator, node_outcome, node_moderator), height = 420)
```

```{r tab-sc-fma}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Mechanism, ~Direction, ~Logic, ~Illustration,
  "Technological leadership", "Advantage", "Learning-curve cost reductions and patents that stay proprietary", "Early leaders in semiconductors riding cumulative output down the cost curve",
  "Pre-emption of scarce assets", "Advantage", "Control of inputs, locations, shelf space, or capacity before rivals", "Retail chains securing the best sites in a new region",
  "Switching costs and network effects", "Advantage", "Buyers who adopt early are costly to lure away, and installed bases attract more users", "eBay's early lead in online auctions in the United States",
  "Free-rider effects", "Disadvantage", "Followers imitate at lower cost and learn from the pioneer's market education", "Platform owners entering categories that complementors have proven",
  "Resolution of uncertainty", "Disadvantage", "Followers enter after technology and demand become clear", "Late entrants building on a settled dominant design",
  "Shifts in technology or needs", "Disadvantage", "The pioneer's assets fit the old technology or needs", "Early social networks overtaken by later entrants",
  "Incumbent inertia", "Disadvantage", "The pioneer becomes locked into early routines and investments", "Early leaders slow to adopt the next technology generation"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Sources of first-mover advantages and disadvantages, following Lieberman and Montgomery (1988).")
```

The core propositions are:

- **P1 (Appropriation).** First movers gain an advantage only when an
  isolating mechanism lets them appropriate the returns of early entry
  [@lieberman1988].
- **P2 (Consumer learning).** In consumer markets, pioneers can shape buyer
  preferences and become the prototype against which later entrants are judged
  [@carpenter1989].
- **P3 (Resources and timing).** The optimal entry time differs across firms
  because firms differ in resources: a firm with strong commercialisation
  capabilities may profit from waiting [@lieberman1998].
- **P4 (Environmental dynamics).** First-mover advantages are most likely when
  both technology and the market evolve smoothly, and least likely when
  technology changes abruptly and overturns the pioneer's position
  [@suarez2007].

### Evidence and extensions

Early evidence was striking. Studies using the Profit Impact of Market Strategy
(PIMS) database found that pioneers held larger market shares than later entrants
[@robinson1985], and reviews of order-of-entry research found an inverse
relationship between order of entry and market share in many consumer product
categories [@kalyanaram1995b]. @carpenter1989 explained why in psychological terms:
the pioneer can define the attributes that consumers consider important.

@golder1993 challenged this record. PIMS and survey studies rely on surviving
firms that classify themselves as pioneers, so failed pioneers vanish from the
data and successful early followers may claim the label. Using historical records
to identify the true pioneers in a set of product categories, Golder and Tellis
found that nearly half had failed and that survivors' average share was much
lower than earlier studies suggested. Early market leaders, who typically
entered after the pioneer, performed better. A meta-analysis by @vanderwerf1997 confirmed that
methodological choices, including the use of market share as the outcome and
the treatment of survivors, shape the observed size of first-mover effects.

@lieberman1998 responded by connecting the theory to
[resource-based theory](#resource-based-theory) (Section \@ref(resource-based-theory)). Entry timing is not an
exogenous treatment but a strategic choice that reflects resources. Firms with
strong technological capabilities may rationally enter early, and firms with
strong marketing and distribution capabilities may rationally wait. Comparing
early and late entrants therefore confounds the effect of timing with the effect
of the resources that led firms to choose that timing.

::: {.debate}
**Marketing logic or marketing legend?** Survivor bias, self-reported pioneer
status, and the endogeneity of entry timing all inflate apparent first-mover
advantages [@golder1993; @vanderwerf1997]. Yet early entry does pay in some
settings, particularly where network effects or switching costs are strong. The
consensus is contingent: first-mover advantages exist but are neither universal
nor automatic [@suarez2007].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Pioneers that held on and pioneers that did not.** eBay, founded in 1995, was
among the earliest online auction sites, and the network effects of a marketplace
(buyers attract sellers and sellers attract buyers) allowed it to dominate U.S.
online auctions for many years. Social networking tells the opposite story.
Friendster and MySpace attracted large audiences before Facebook, yet Facebook
overtook both. Similarly, Google entered web search years after AltaVista and
Yahoo. The mechanisms in Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-fma) explain the difference.
Where network effects were strong and technology stable, the pioneer's lead
persisted. Where technology and user expectations shifted rapidly, better
followers free-rode on the market education that pioneers had provided.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Platform entry decisions.** Platform owners face a recurring timing choice:
whether, and when, to enter the product spaces of their own complementors. @zhu2018
studied Amazon's entry into product categories previously served by third-party
sellers on its marketplace and found that Amazon was more likely to enter product
spaces that had already proved popular and well rated. In the language of
first-mover theory, the platform deliberately waits, allowing complementors to
resolve market uncertainty, and then enters as a well-informed follower. For
complementors, the implication is that being first on a platform carries a
distinctive risk: success itself signals an attractive category to the
platform owner.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The market-share advantage of pioneers over early followers will be
  larger in categories with strong network effects than in categories without
  them.
- *H2.* After controlling for the selection of entry timing on firm resources,
  the effect of early entry on long-run survival will be smaller than in naive
  comparisons.

**Designs.** Historical identification of all entrants (including failures),
selection models or instrumental variables for entry timing, matched comparisons
of pioneers and followers with similar resources, and consumer experiments on
pioneer prototypicality.

**Measures.** Order and date of entry, survival, long-run market share and
profitability, switching-cost and network-effect proxies, pace of technical
change (patent or performance-improvement rates).
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Survivor bias.** Studying only firms that still exist, or relying on firms to
report whether they pioneered a market, systematically overstates first-mover
advantages. Build the sample of entrants from historical sources before
outcomes are known, include failures, and treat entry timing as a choice that
must be modelled rather than as a random treatment.
:::

## Real Options Theory {#real-options-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Many strategic investments create the right, but not the
obligation, to take future actions. When the future is uncertain and investments
are irreversible, such **real options** have value that static net present
value ignores. Firms should invest small amounts to create options, keep them
open while uncertainty resolves, and exercise or abandon them as information
arrives.

**Origins.** Finance and strategic management. @myers1977 framed growth
opportunities as options on real assets. @dixit1994 and @trigeorgis1996 developed
the theory of investment under uncertainty. Strategy applications by
@kogut1991, @bowman1993, @mcgrath1997, and @mcgrath1999. Boundaries examined by
@adner2004, reviewed by @trigeorgis2017.

**Level of analysis.** Investment project and the firm's portfolio of
investments.

**Key constructs.** Uncertainty (volatility), irreversibility, flexibility,
option to defer, stage, expand, abandon, or switch, exercise decision, growth
options, option value.

**Boundary conditions.** Uncertainty must be resolvable over time through
external events or the firm's own learning. The investment must be at least
partly irreversible. Managers must be able and willing to exercise or abandon
options on the basis of new information.

**Related theories.** [Behavioral theory of the firm](#behavioral-theory-of-the-firm),
[Escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment) (Section \@ref(escalation-of-commitment)),
[Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)),
[Portfolio theory](#portfolio-theory) (Section \@ref(portfolio-theory)),
[Effectuation](#effectuation) (Section \@ref(effectuation)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

@myers1977 observed that much of a firm's value consists of **growth
opportunities**: options to make future investments whose value depends on
conditions not yet known. Treating them as call options on real assets gave rise
to the term **real options**. Just as a call option gives the right to buy an
asset at a fixed price, an R&D project, pilot plant, or joint venture gives a
firm the right to invest more later if conditions prove favourable.

@dixit1994 developed the economic theory. Their key result is that when an
investment is irreversible and its value uncertain, the option to wait has
value, so the firm should invest only when the expected value exceeds the
investment cost by a margin that grows with uncertainty. The textbook rule
"invest if NPV > 0" is wrong in such settings, because investing now *kills* the
option to wait. @trigeorgis1996 catalogued the main types of real options, which
Table \@ref(tab:tab-sc-options) summarises.

```{r tab-sc-options}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Option type`, ~`What it allows`, ~`Business example`,
  "Option to defer", "Wait for uncertainty to resolve before committing", "Holding land or a licence without developing it",
  "Option to stage", "Invest in sequential steps, each conditional on the last", "Drug development through clinical phases, venture capital rounds",
  "Option to expand (growth option)", "Scale up if the market proves attractive", "Pilot plant, test-market launch, platform entry into a small market",
  "Option to abandon", "Exit and recover salvage value if outcomes are poor", "Leasing rather than buying assets, kill criteria in R&D",
  "Option to switch", "Change inputs, outputs, or processes as prices change", "Flexible manufacturing lines, dual-fuel power plants",
  "Option to acquire", "Buy out a partner when value becomes clear", "Joint ventures that end in acquisition"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Types of real options and business examples (organized following Trigeorgis, 1996).")
```

### Core logic and propositions

Real options reasoning makes three counterintuitive predictions. First,
uncertainty can *increase* the value of an investment opportunity, because the
option holder captures the upside and limits the downside. Second, small initial
investments that look unprofitable on their own can be justified by the options
they create. Third, the value of flexibility is greatest when uncertainty is high
and when information arrives before the major commitment must be made. Figure
\@ref(fig:fig-sc-option) illustrates the second and third points.

```{r fig-sc-option, fig.cap = "Stylised comparison of committing to a full investment now with staging it through a pilot. The full project has a static NPV of -5 at every level of uncertainty. Staging costs 5 up front but lets the firm scale only if the pilot reveals a favourable market. The value of staging rises with uncertainty, and above a threshold the staged project is worth undertaking even though the full project is not. Illustrative Monte Carlo values.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1977)
v0 <- 100; invest <- 105; pilot <- 5
z <- rnorm(20000)
option_df <- tibble::tibble(sigma = seq(0, 0.8, by = 0.02)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(staged = mean(pmax(v0 * exp(sigma * z - sigma^2 / 2) - invest, 0)) - pilot) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(commit = v0 - invest) |>
  pivot_longer(c(staged, commit), names_to = "strategy", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(strategy = recode(strategy, staged = "Stage: pilot first, scale only if favourable",
                           commit = "Commit to full investment now (static NPV)"))
threshold <- option_df |> filter(strategy == "Stage: pilot first, scale only if favourable", value > 0) |>
  summarise(s = min(sigma)) |> pull(s)
ggplot(option_df, aes(sigma, value, colour = strategy)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = threshold, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = threshold + 0.01, y = 22, hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "Staging becomes worth\nundertaking above this\nlevel of uncertainty") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["orange"]], pal[["blue"]])) +
  labs(x = "Uncertainty about project value (volatility)", y = "Expected value (stylised units)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Uncertainty raises the value of staged investment",
       caption = "Stylised: project value 100, full investment 105, pilot cost 5, lognormal value revealed by the pilot.") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1))
```

In propositional form:

- **P1 (Value of flexibility).** The value of an option to invest increases with
  the uncertainty of the underlying opportunity and with the time available
  before the decision must be made [@dixit1994].
- **P2 (Staging).** Under high uncertainty, firms that invest in small, staged
  steps outperform firms that commit fully at the outset, provided that they
  abandon unpromising options [@mcgrath1999].
- **P3 (Option chains).** Initial investments create **shadow options** that
  become recognised and valued only as firms learn, and options often come in
  chains in which exercising one creates the next [@bowman1993].
- **P4 (Acquisition timing).** Firms structure uncertain collaborations as joint
  ventures and exercise the option to acquire when the venture's value turns out
  to be higher than expected [@kogut1991].

### Evidence and extensions

@bowman1993 recast strategy as an **incremental-choice process** in which firms
build portfolios of options through small resource investments and strike them
when opportunities become clear. @kogut1991 found that unexpected increases in
the value of a joint venture's product market made acquisition by a partner more
likely, consistent with the venture serving as an option to expand.
@mcgrath1999 argued that options reasoning reframes entrepreneurial failure as an
expected outcome of a portfolio: the goal is to bound the cost of each failure and
multiply the number of attempts, so that occasional large successes pay for many
small losses.

@adner2004 argued that real options logic is often misapplied. Financial options
have fixed underlying assets and exercise prices, whereas real projects can be
redefined along the way: when a technology disappoints, managers can always find
a new application for it, which undermines the discipline of abandonment. A
review by @trigeorgis2017 concludes that the theory is well supported where
staging is clear (R&D, joint ventures, international expansion) but that
measurement of option value and of managers' actual reasoning remains weak.

::: {.debate}
**Options or escalation?** Real options reasoning assumes that managers will kill
options when signals are negative. Behavioural research on
[escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment) (Section \@ref(escalation-of-commitment)) suggests that they often do
not. Pilots become pet projects, sunk costs create pressure to continue, and the
language of options can be used to justify investments that would otherwise be
rejected. Critics also question whether real options valuation, built for traded
financial assets, is meaningful when the underlying asset is not traded and its
volatility cannot be estimated [@adner2004]. Proponents respond that the main
value of the theory is *reasoning*, not precise valuation: framing decisions as
options changes how firms structure investments, set milestones, and define
abandonment criteria [@mcgrath1999].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Staged R&D in pharmaceuticals.** Drug development is a sequence of options.
Discovery and preclinical work buy the right to start human trials, Phase I
trials buy the right to conduct Phase II, and so on through Phase III and
regulatory review. Each stage typically costs more than the last and resolves
part of the technical and commercial uncertainty, and most candidates are
abandoned along the way. A static valuation that ignores the right to stop
understates the value of early-stage candidates. Staged venture capital rounds
follow the same logic.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: entering a new market through a pilot.** A
consumer-goods firm is considering an irreversible factory investment in a new
national market with highly uncertain demand and a slightly negative static NPV.
Options reasoning suggests an import-and-distribution pilot with a local partner,
explicit milestones (sales volume, retailer reorders), and a factory only if the
milestones are met. The decisive question is whether the firm will actually walk
away if they are missed.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Firms will be more likely to use joint ventures rather than acquisitions
  to enter markets with high demand uncertainty.
- *H2.* The likelihood of acquiring a joint-venture partner will increase after
  positive, unexpected shocks to the venture's market value.
- *H3.* R&D projects with pre-specified kill criteria will be abandoned earlier
  after negative signals than projects without such criteria.

**Measures.** Uncertainty (volatility of industry returns, forecast dispersion),
irreversibility (asset specificity, sunk-cost share), staging (number of
investment rounds, milestone contracts), exercise and abandonment events.

**Designs.** Event histories of entry mode and exercise decisions (alliance
databases, clinical trial registries, venture financing rounds), laboratory
experiments on abandonment, and simulation models of option portfolios.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Calling everything an option.** Any investment can be described as creating
future opportunities, so the label "option" can rationalise almost anything. A
real option exists only if uncertainty will resolve before the next decision,
the next decision is genuinely discretionary, and the firm is prepared to abandon
the position. If a pilot cannot produce decision-relevant information, or if the
organization will never walk away, it is not an option but a down payment on a
commitment already made [@adner2004].
:::

## Behavioral Theory of the Firm {#behavioral-theory-of-the-firm}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Firms are coalitions of boundedly rational actors that pursue
multiple goals expressed as **aspiration levels**. When performance falls below
aspiration, firms engage in **problemistic search** and become more willing to
change. When performance exceeds aspiration, **slack** accumulates and change is
driven more by slack and less by problems. Aspirations adapt to past performance
and to the performance of peers.

**Origins.** Organization theory and economics at the Carnegie Institute of
Technology. @cyert1963, building on @simon1955. Performance feedback theory
developed by @greve1998 and @greve2003. Reviewed by @gavetti2012 and @shinkle2012.

**Level of analysis.** Organization, with micro-foundations in individual and
group decision making.

**Key constructs.** Organizational coalition, aspiration level (historical and
social), performance feedback, problemistic search, slack search, organizational
slack, quasi-resolution of conflict, uncertainty avoidance, standard operating
procedures, adaptive learning.

**Boundary conditions.** Goals must be measurable and salient. The theory assumes
that decision makers compare performance with reference points and that search is
costly. Predictions weaken near the point of organizational survival, where
attention shifts from aspirations to avoiding failure [@march1992].

**Related theories.** [Bounded rationality](#bounded-rationality) (Section \@ref(bounded-rationality)),
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory-model) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-model)),
[Organizational learning](#organizational-learning) (Section \@ref(organizational-learning)),
[Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)),
[Attention-based view](#attention-based-view),
[Garbage can model](#garbage-can-model) (Section \@ref(garbage-can-model)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Neoclassical economics treated the firm as a single actor maximising profit with
complete information. @cyert1963 replaced this abstraction with a model of how
real firms make decisions about price, output, and resource allocation. Building
on @simon1955's concept of **[bounded rationality](#bounded-rationality) (Section \@ref(bounded-rationality))**, they described the firm as a
**coalition** of participants (managers, workers, shareholders, suppliers) with
partly conflicting goals. Goals are not maximised but expressed as aspiration
levels: targets that define satisfactory performance. Four relational concepts
organized the theory:

- **Quasi-resolution of conflict.** Conflicting goals are attended to
  sequentially and in separate subunits rather than reconciled.
- **Uncertainty avoidance.** Firms prefer short-run feedback and negotiated
  environments to long-run forecasting.
- **Problemistic search.** Search is triggered by problems, begins near the
  symptom and current alternatives, and is biased by searchers' experience.
- **Organizational learning.** Goals and search rules adapt to experience.

**Organizational slack**, the excess of available resources over the payments
needed to hold the coalition together, absorbs shocks, eases conflict, and funds
experiments that would not survive scrutiny in lean times
[@cyert1963; @bourgeois1981].

### Core logic and propositions

Modern performance feedback theory formalises the model. Each period the firm
compares its performance with an aspiration level that is a weighted average of
its own past performance (the **historical aspiration**) and the performance of
comparable firms (the **social aspiration**). Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-btof) shows
the loop.

```{r fig-sc-btof, fig.cap = "The behavioral theory of the firm as a performance feedback loop. Performance is compared with an aspiration level formed from the firm's own history and from peers. Shortfalls trigger problemistic search and greater willingness to take risks. Success builds slack, which funds slack search. Aspirations then adapt to experience."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  P  [label = "Performance", %s]
  H  [label = "Historical\\naspiration\\n(own past)", %s]
  S  [label = "Social aspiration\\n(peer performance)", %s]
  G  [label = "Performance relative\\nto aspiration", %s]
  PS [label = "Problemistic search\\n(below aspiration)", %s]
  SL [label = "Slack and slack search\\n(above aspiration)", %s]
  C  [label = "Risky change\\n(new products, markets,\\nacquisitions)", %s]
  P -> G
  H -> G
  S -> G
  G -> PS
  G -> SL
  PS -> C
  SL -> C [style = dashed]
  C -> P [label = " future\\n performance", constraint = false]
  P -> H [style = dotted, label = " updating", constraint = false]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism,
   node_mechanism, node_outcome), height = 360)
```

The main propositions are:

- **P1 (Problemistic search).** The further performance falls below aspiration,
  the more intensively firms search for solutions and the more willing they are
  to make risky changes [@cyert1963; @greve1998].
- **P2 (Success and persistence).** As performance rises above aspiration, the
  likelihood of risky change declines, and past success breeds strategic
  persistence [@audia2000].
- **P3 (Slack).** Slack enables experimentation, so the relationship between
  slack and innovation is positive up to a point, beyond which slack breeds
  complacency and undisciplined projects [@nohria1996].
- **P4 (Adaptive aspirations).** Aspirations adjust toward recent own and peer
  performance, so persistent success raises the bar and persistent failure
  lowers it.
- **P5 (Survival focus).** Near the threshold of failure, attention can shift
  from the aspiration to survival, making firms more cautious than performance
  feedback alone would predict [@march1988; @march1992].

Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-feedback) shows the stylised shape that performance
feedback research typically estimates.

```{r fig-sc-feedback, fig.cap = "Stylised performance feedback relationship. The probability of a risky strategic change declines as performance rises relative to aspiration, with a change in slope (a kink) at the aspiration level. Points show binned averages from simulated firm-years, and the line shows the generating function. Illustrative data.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1963)
n_fy <- 4000
gap <- rnorm(n_fy, 0, 1)                                   # performance minus aspiration (standardised)
eta <- ifelse(gap < 0, -1.6 - 0.9 * gap, -1.6 - 0.35 * gap)
change <- rbinom(n_fy, 1, plogis(eta))
