binned <- tibble::tibble(gap, change) |>
  mutate(bin = cut(gap, breaks = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.5))) |>
  filter(!is.na(bin)) |>
  group_by(bin) |>
  summarise(gap = mean(gap), rate = mean(change), n = n())
curve_df <- tibble::tibble(gap = seq(-3, 3, by = 0.02)) |>
  mutate(p = plogis(ifelse(gap < 0, -1.6 - 0.9 * gap, -1.6 - 0.35 * gap)))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -3, xmax = 0, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["orange"]], alpha = 0.06) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(data = curve_df, aes(gap, p), colour = pal[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(data = binned, aes(gap, rate), colour = ink[["secondary"]], size = 2.2) +
  annotate("text", x = -1.5, y = 0.62, label = "Below aspiration:\nproblemistic search", size = 3.3, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.35, label = "Above aspiration:\nslack and persistence", size = 3.3, colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 0.75)) +
  labs(x = "Performance relative to aspiration (standardised)", y = "Probability of risky change",
       title = "Performance shortfalls trigger change",
       caption = "Illustrative simulation: 4,000 firm-years, piecewise logit with a kink at the aspiration level.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

Performance feedback is one of the best-supported predictions in organization
theory. @greve1998 studied U.S. radio stations and found that stations were more
likely to make risky changes of format when performance fell short of
aspirations and less likely as performance rose above them, using both
historical and social aspiration levels. @greve2003 synthesised the program
into a general theory of learning from performance feedback. Similar patterns
appear for corporate risk taking [@bromiley1991] and acquisitions
[@iyer2008]. @audia2000 combined an archival study of firms facing deregulation
with a laboratory study to show that past success increases strategic persistence
after radical environmental change, even when persistence hurts performance.
@nohria1996 found an inverted-U relationship between slack and innovation: too
little slack starves experimentation, whereas too much reduces discipline.

The theory's reference-point logic parallels
[prospect theory](#prospect-theory-model) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-model)) [@kahneman1979], and its account of
local search anticipates the trade-off between
[exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)) [@march1991] and the
**myopia of learning** [@levinthal1993]. Reviews call for more attention to
multiple, conflicting goals and to how firms choose the comparison group that
defines their social aspiration [@gavetti2012; @shinkle2012].

::: {.debate}
**Search or threat rigidity?** The BTOF predicts that failure stimulates search
and risk taking. A competing view holds that threat produces rigidity: under
pressure, organizations centralise control and fall back on familiar routines.
The two can be reconciled through the survival point [@march1992]: moderate
shortfalls trigger search, whereas threats to survival trigger caution. A second
debate concerns measurement. Aspiration levels are rarely observed and are
usually computed from historical and peer performance with assumed weights, so
results can be sensitive to how aspirations are constructed [@shinkle2012].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Performance-feedback-driven change.** The theory explains a familiar
corporate pattern. Firms that miss their own targets, or fall behind peers, are
more likely to reorganise, replace executives, launch acquisitions, or change
strategy [@greve1998; @iyer2008]. Firms that beat expectations tend to persist,
which is efficient when the environment is stable and dangerous when it is
not. @audia2000 showed that after deregulation transformed industries such as
airlines and trucking, previously successful firms were slower to change their
strategies. Practical implications follow. Managers can deliberately set
aspirations by choosing comparison groups (a firm benchmarked against a
struggling peer group will feel little pressure to change), and boards can
counteract success-induced persistence by commissioning reviews when
performance is strong rather than only when it is weak.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The likelihood of a strategic change will increase as performance falls
  further below the social aspiration level.
- *H2.* Performance above aspiration will reduce the likelihood of risky change,
  and this effect will be weaker for firms with high absorbed slack.
- *H3.* The effect of performance shortfalls on risk taking will reverse as firms
  approach the threshold of financial distress.

**Measures.** Historical aspiration (exponentially weighted own past
performance), social aspiration (peer mean or median), performance-aspiration
gaps (spline coded above and below zero), slack (current ratio, selling and
administrative expense ratio, unused borrowing capacity), and risky change (R&D
intensity, acquisitions, entry into new markets, product changes).

**Designs.** Panel models with spline specifications at the aspiration level,
event-history models of change, laboratory experiments that manipulate feedback,
and agent-based simulations of aspiration adaptation.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Mechanical aspirations.** Researchers often compute aspirations with arbitrary
weights and comparison groups and then treat the resulting gap as an observed
psychological reference point. Results can change with the weights. Report
sensitivity to alternative specifications, justify the peer group, and where
possible validate aspirations against stated targets (guidance, budgets,
incentive thresholds).
:::

## Attention-Based View {#attention-based-view}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Firm behaviour is the result of how organizations channel and
distribute the attention of their decision makers. What managers notice, and
therefore what the firm does, depends on the issues and answers they focus on,
the situation they find themselves in, and the rules, resources, and
relationships that structure attention within the firm.

**Origins.** Strategic management and organization theory. @ocasio1997, building
on @simon1955 and @cyert1963, refined in @ocasio2011.

**Level of analysis.** Organization and individual decision makers, linked
through the firm's structures and communication channels.

**Key constructs.** Focus of attention, situated attention, structural
distribution of attention, issues and answers, attention structures (rules of the
game, players, structural positions, resources), procedural and communication
channels, organizational moves.

**Boundary conditions.** Attention must be scarce relative to the issues
competing for it. The view is most useful when outcomes depend on noticing and
interpreting change rather than on executing a known plan.

**Related theories.** [Behavioral theory of the firm](#behavioral-theory-of-the-firm),
[Upper echelons theory](#upper-echelons-theory) (Section \@ref(upper-echelons-theory)),
[Sensemaking](#sensemaking) (Section \@ref(sensemaking)),
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework)),
[Strategic groups](#strategic-groups).
:::

### Core logic

If rationality is bounded, attention is the scarce resource. @ocasio1997 built a
theory of the firm on three principles. **Focus of attention**: what decision
makers do depends on the issues and answers they focus on. **Situated
attention**: that focus depends on the context in front of them (meetings,
reports, problems). **Structural distribution of attention**: the firm's rules,
resources, players, and positions determine which issues reach which decision
makers, through **procedural and communication channels** such as budget
reviews, planning cycles, and executive committees. Organizational moves are the
output of this attention-processing system (Figure \@ref(fig:fig-sc-abv)).

```{r fig-sc-abv, fig.cap = "The attention-based view. The environment and the firm's attention structures (rules, players, positions, resources) feed issues and answers into procedural and communication channels. These channels situate the attention of decision makers, whose focus determines organizational moves, which in turn reshape the environment and the firm's structures."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  ENV [label = "Environment of\\ndecisions", %s]
  AS  [label = "Attention structures\\n(rules, players,\\npositions, resources)", %s]
  CH  [label = "Procedural and\\ncommunication channels\\n(reviews, planning, committees)", %s]
  DM  [label = "Situated attention of\\ndecision makers\\n(issues and answers)", %s]
  MV  [label = "Organizational\\nmoves", %s]
  ENV -> CH
  AS -> CH
  CH -> DM
  AS -> DM [style = dashed]
  DM -> MV
  MV -> ENV [style = dashed, constraint = false]
  MV -> AS [style = dashed, constraint = false]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome), height = 340)
```

The view yields three core propositions:

- **P1 (Selective focus).** Firms respond to the environmental changes that their
  decision makers attend to, not to all changes that matter [@ocasio1997].
- **P2 (Structure channels attention).** The design of governance channels,
  committees, and reporting systems shapes which issues reach top management and
  therefore which adaptations occur [@joseph2012].
- **P3 (Executive attention and adaptation).** When top managers attend to an
  emerging technology or market, firms adapt faster
  [@eggers2009; @cho2006].

### Evidence and extensions

@cho2006 studied U.S. airlines after the 1978 deregulation and found that the
composition of top management teams influenced the extent to which executives
attended to entrepreneurial issues, and that this attention mediated the
relationship between team characteristics and strategic change. @eggers2009
found that incumbent communications-equipment firms entered the emerging
optical networking market faster when their CEOs paid more attention to the new
technology. @joseph2012 traced half a century of General Electric's history and
showed that the architecture of cross-level governance channels shaped how the
firm's attention, and with it adaptation, evolved. @tripsas2000 showed that
Polaroid developed strong digital imaging capabilities but that managerial beliefs
anchored in its instant-film business model directed attention away from
commercialising them. @ocasio2011 refined the theory by distinguishing
**attentional perspective** (the top-down schemas that make some issues salient),
**attentional engagement** (sustained, effortful allocation of attention), and
**attentional selection** (the outcome of the process).

::: {.debate}
**Attention or cognition?** Attention is hard to observe, and common proxies
such as word counts in shareholder letters may reflect impression management.
The view also overlaps with upper echelons theory, sensemaking, and managerial
cognition. Its distinctive contribution is the *structural* claim: attention is
distributed by the organization's channels and rules, not only by executives'
personal characteristics [@ocasio2011; @joseph2012].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Redirecting a firm's attention.** In May 1995, Bill Gates circulated an
internal memo titled "The Internet Tidal Wave," which declared the internet the
most important development for Microsoft since the IBM PC and directed managers
across the company to make it a priority. Whatever one concludes about the
subsequent strategy, the memo is a clear instance of a deliberate attempt to
change the **focus of attention** of an entire organization. Intel offers a
complementary structural example. @burgelman1994 showed that Intel's exit from
dynamic memory chips in the mid-1980s was prepared by middle managers who
allocated scarce manufacturing capacity according to a margin-per-wafer rule,
which steadily shifted resources toward microprocessors before top management
formally decided to exit. The resource-allocation rule was an attention structure
that channelled the firm toward its future.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Firms whose top executives devote more attention to an emerging
  technology in public communications will enter the technology's market
  sooner.
- *H2.* The creation of a dedicated governance channel for a new issue (for
  example, a sustainability committee of the board) will increase the firm's
  subsequent investment in that issue.
- *H3.* Attention to competitors in executive communications will mediate the
  effect of market commonality on competitive responses.

**Measures.** Text-based attention measures from shareholder letters, earnings
calls, and internal documents, agenda analysis of meetings, the structure of
committees and reporting lines, time allocation of executives.

**Designs.** Longitudinal case studies of attention structures, panel models
with text-based attention measures, and natural experiments in which reporting
structures change.
:::

## Chapter Summary {#strategy-competition-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- The **structure-conduct-performance** paradigm explains profit differences by
  industry structure and entry barriers [@bain1956]. Variance-decomposition
  studies show that industry matters, but that firm-specific effects often matter
  more [@rumelt1991; @mcgahan1997].
- **Strategic groups** and **mobility barriers** explain persistent differences
  among firms within the same industry [@caves1977], although the existence and
  performance consequences of groups remain contested [@barney1990].
- **Competitive dynamics** treats rivalry as action and response between specific
  rivals, shaped by market commonality, resource similarity, and the
  awareness-motivation-capability drivers. Multimarket contact can produce
  **mutual forbearance** [@chen1996; @gimeno1999].
- **Game theory** identifies the structure of strategic interaction. One-shot
  dilemmas produce mutual defection, repeated interaction and credible
  commitment can sustain cooperation or deter entry [@nash1950; @dixit1980].
- **First-mover advantages** are real but contingent on isolating mechanisms,
  resources, and environmental dynamics, and early evidence was inflated by survivor
  bias [@lieberman1988; @golder1993].
- **Real options theory** shows why uncertainty and irreversibility make
  staged investment valuable, provided that firms are willing to abandon
  options [@dixit1994; @mcgrath1999; @adner2004].
- The **behavioral theory of the firm** explains change as a response to
  performance relative to aspirations, with slack and search as central
  mechanisms [@cyert1963; @greve2003].
- The **attention-based view** explains firm behaviour by how organizations
  structure and distribute the attention of decision makers [@ocasio1997].
:::

## Discussion Questions {#strategy-competition-questions}

1. Variance-decomposition studies reach different conclusions about how much
   industry matters. What features of the data and research design drive these
   differences, and what would a design that identifies the *causal* effect of
   industry structure on profitability look like?
2. Choose an industry you know well and draw a strategic group map. Which
   mobility barriers separate the groups, and which firms are best placed to
   cross them?
3. Using the awareness-motivation-capability framework, predict how incumbent
   carriers would respond to the entry of a low-cost airline into one of their hub
   markets. How would multimarket contact change your prediction?
4. The cola rivalry has involved intense advertising but relatively few sustained
   list-price wars. Use repeated-game logic to explain why, and identify the
   conditions under which a price war would become more likely.
5. Golder and Tellis argued that pioneering advantage was partly a "marketing
   legend." Design a study of entry timing in a recent technology market that
   avoids survivor bias and accounts for the endogeneity of entry timing.
6. A manager argues that every pilot project is a real option. Under what
   conditions is she right, and how would you design governance (milestones, kill
   criteria) so that the options logic and the behavioural tendency toward
   escalation do not conflict?

## Further Reading {#strategy-competition-reading}

- @bain1956: the classic statement of entry barriers and the foundation of the
  industrial-organization approach to strategy.
- @rumelt1991 and @mcgahan1997: the central exchange in the "how much does
  industry matter?" debate. Read them together.
- @chen1996: an integrative theory of competitor analysis that introduced market
  commonality, resource similarity, and competitor asymmetry.
- @brandenburger1996: an accessible translation of game theory into managerial
  strategy, built around the value net and the idea of changing the game.
- @lieberman1988 and @golder1993: the theoretical case for first-mover advantages
  and the most influential methodological critique of the evidence.
- @mcgrath1999 and @adner2004: the case for real options reasoning in
  entrepreneurship and a careful statement of its boundaries.
- @cyert1963 and @gavetti2012: the founding text of the behavioral theory of the
  firm and a modern assessment of its legacy and prospects.
- @ocasio1997: the original statement of the attention-based view, with a
  framework that remains the starting point for research on organizational
  attention.
